items.prompt: A security team wants managed detection of suspicious AWS account and workload activity without writing its own event-correlation engine. Which service is the direct fit?
constraints: The team needs threat detection rather than only configuration compliance.
The organization can enable supported data sources.
Findings need an incident workflow.

options.text: Use Amazon GuardDuty for managed threat detection and route its findings into the organization's response workflow.
Use Amazon Inspector because Inspector is the primary service for behavioral account-threat detection.
Use AWS Config alone because configuration history automatically identifies every active threat.
Use CloudFormation because stacks contain all runtime security telemetry.

feedback.Reason: GuardDuty is the managed AWS threat-detection service, while Inspector focuses on vulnerability exposure and Config on resource configuration state.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: GuardDuty analyzes supported account, workload, and data signals to produce security findings. It does not replace vulnerability scanning, compliance configuration, or incident response.
Details.scenarioApplication: The security account enables GuardDuty, configures member-account administration, and sends findings to Security Hub or the response system.
Details.errorCorrection: Inspector is not the general behavioral threat detector, Config is not a complete active-threat engine, and CloudFormation is deployment state.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Managed detection reduces custom analytics work but requires finding triage, coverage review, and response ownership.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Inspector primarily assesses software and resource vulnerabilities rather than serving as the general threat-detection engine.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Config records and evaluates configuration compliance, not every active threat signal.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: CloudFormation describes infrastructure and does not contain runtime threat telemetry.

items.prompt: GuardDuty does not produce a finding for an activity the team expected it to see. What coverage question should be asked first?
constraints: The finding type depends on a supported GuardDuty data source.
The account and Region are enabled.
The team can inspect service configuration and event evidence.

options.text: Verify that GuardDuty is enabled in the affected account and Region and that the relevant protection plan or data source is enabled and supported for the event.
Assume GuardDuty inspects every packet, API call, file, and application log automatically without coverage configuration.
Disable CloudTrail because GuardDuty findings require no account activity history.
Use an IAM permission boundary to add a missing GuardDuty detection source.

feedback.Reason: Threat-detection findings depend on account, Region, and feature coverage, so an expected finding requires a coverage check before rule changes.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: GuardDuty protection plans and data sources vary by service and event type. Enabling the detector alone does not mean every optional source or workload is covered.
Details.scenarioApplication: The operator checks detector status, protection plans, member-account configuration, and the underlying event before declaring a detection gap.
Details.errorCorrection: No service inspects every possible signal automatically, CloudTrail is an important account activity source, and IAM boundaries do not add GuardDuty features.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Broader protection increases coverage and cost, so the organization should document the detection contract and exclusions.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: GuardDuty coverage is feature- and data-source-specific rather than universal inspection of every signal.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Disabling account activity telemetry can remove evidence needed by threat detection.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Permission boundaries govern IAM permissions and do not enable GuardDuty protection plans.

items.prompt: The organization needs GuardDuty to identify suspicious access patterns against sensitive S3 data. Which capability should be evaluated?
constraints: The buckets are in monitored accounts.
The team can enable the relevant GuardDuty S3 protection.
S3 access policy review remains separate.

options.text: Enable the supported GuardDuty S3 protection feature and investigate its findings alongside S3 policy, CloudTrail, and data-owner evidence.
Use Inspector because it scans every S3 object for malicious user behavior by default.
Use an S3 lifecycle rule because lifecycle transitions detect suspicious reads.
Make the bucket public so GuardDuty can observe access from all clients.

feedback.Reason: GuardDuty offers S3 protection coverage, while the bucket's authorization and retention policies remain distinct controls.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: GuardDuty can analyze supported S3 data-event activity when the protection plan is enabled. Findings identify suspicious behavior but do not rewrite the bucket policy or prove a breach alone.
Details.scenarioApplication: The security team enables S3 protection for the intended accounts, correlates findings with CloudTrail data events, and preserves bucket-owner context.
Details.errorCorrection: Inspector is not the S3 behavioral detector, lifecycle rules manage objects rather than threat analytics, and public exposure is not required.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: S3 data-event monitoring improves visibility but creates additional event volume and cost that should be scoped to sensitive buckets.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Inspector's vulnerability scope is different from GuardDuty S3 threat detection.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Lifecycle transitions do not analyze suspicious access behavior.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Monitoring should be enabled without making a sensitive bucket public.

items.prompt: A team wants runtime threat detection for suspicious activity in EKS workloads, not only container-image CVEs. Which service capability should be evaluated?
constraints: The cluster and Region support the relevant feature.
The team distinguishes runtime behavior from image vulnerabilities.
Findings must identify the affected workload context.

options.text: Evaluate the relevant GuardDuty EKS or runtime protection feature and keep Inspector responsible for its separate vulnerability-assessment scope.
Use Inspector alone because an image vulnerability scan detects every runtime compromise.
Use a Kubernetes security group because security groups inspect process behavior inside pods.
Disable EKS audit logging because GuardDuty needs no workload or cluster evidence.

feedback.Reason: GuardDuty and Inspector answer different questions: runtime threat behavior versus vulnerability exposure.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: GuardDuty EKS protection analyzes supported Kubernetes or runtime signals, while Inspector assesses supported software and image vulnerabilities. Both can feed a broader security workflow.
Details.scenarioApplication: The platform team enables the required GuardDuty protection, keeps image scanning active, and maps each finding type to an owner.
Details.errorCorrection: An image scan does not observe every runtime compromise, security groups do not inspect processes, and disabling audit evidence reduces coverage.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Runtime protection increases visibility and cost; the organization should scope clusters and retain the logs needed for investigation.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Inspector vulnerability results do not replace runtime threat detection.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Security groups are network filters and do not inspect pod process behavior.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Cluster audit or runtime evidence can be part of the detection coverage and should not be removed casually.

items.prompt: A security team needs continuously refreshed findings about software vulnerabilities in EC2, ECR images, and Lambda packages. Which service is the direct fit?
constraints: The team needs vulnerability exposure, not active behavior analytics.
The resources are in supported scope.
Findings should include severity and remediation context.

options.text: Use Amazon Inspector for supported continuous vulnerability assessment of the selected compute and image resources.
Use GuardDuty because GuardDuty is the managed CVE scanner for every software artifact.
Use Detective because Detective installs vulnerability scanners on every EC2 instance.
Use Route 53 because DNS health checks identify vulnerable package versions.

feedback.Reason: Inspector focuses on vulnerability assessment for supported resource types, unlike GuardDuty's threat-detection focus.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Inspector analyzes supported package, image, and workload exposure and produces findings with vulnerability context. It does not determine whether a credential was actively abused.
Details.scenarioApplication: The security team enables the relevant resource scans, prioritizes exploitable findings, and assigns patch or image owners.
Details.errorCorrection: GuardDuty is not the general CVE scanner, Detective provides investigation context rather than scanning, and DNS health checks do not inspect packages.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Continuous assessment improves freshness but requires coverage, patch ownership, and vulnerability-prioritization processes.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: GuardDuty detects suspicious activity; Inspector is the vulnerability-assessment service.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Detective analyzes investigation context and does not install a universal vulnerability scanner.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: DNS health checks measure endpoint health and do not inspect software packages.

items.prompt: Inspector reports an EC2 package vulnerability, and the team wants to prioritize instances that are reachable from the internet. Which evidence is useful?
constraints: Inspector produces the vulnerability finding.
The team can inspect network exposure and package severity.
Priority should reflect exploitability and impact.

options.text: Correlate the Inspector finding with its network-reachability or exposure evidence, asset criticality, and remediation availability before prioritizing the patch.
Patch every finding in arbitrary order because network exposure never changes vulnerability risk.
Use GuardDuty to rewrite the package version because threat findings automatically patch EC2.
Change the IAM role to make the vulnerable package disappear from Inspector inventory.

feedback.Reason: Inspector findings can be prioritized with exposure, severity, asset importance, and remediation context rather than severity alone.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A vulnerability finding describes package exposure; network reachability and workload criticality add context for remediation order. The service reports evidence but does not silently patch the instance.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner ranks internet-reachable critical assets first, validates the fix, and tracks residual findings after the package update.
Details.errorCorrection: Arbitrary order ignores risk context, GuardDuty does not patch packages, and IAM changes do not remove a software vulnerability from inventory.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Risk-based prioritization improves remediation value but requires reliable asset ownership and network-exposure evidence.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Severity alone is not the complete risk context when exposure and asset impact differ.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: GuardDuty findings do not automatically update EC2 packages.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: IAM role changes do not change the installed package version or vulnerability state.

items.prompt: A CI pipeline should prevent deployment of a container image with a critical OS-package vulnerability. Which control should be evaluated?
constraints: Images are stored in ECR.
The build can inspect findings before deployment.
The production cluster should not be the first discovery point.

options.text: Use Inspector ECR scanning and make the deployment pipeline evaluate the resulting vulnerability severity before promoting the image.
Use GuardDuty because it blocks every vulnerable image before it is pushed to ECR.
Use a security group because image package content is determined by inbound network rules.
Use CloudFront because edge caching removes vulnerabilities from container layers.

feedback.Reason: Inspector ECR scanning produces image vulnerability findings that can become a promotion gate when the pipeline consumes them.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Inspector analyzes supported ECR images and reports package vulnerabilities. The pipeline or deployment policy must decide whether a severity or age threshold blocks promotion.
Details.scenarioApplication: The build scans the immutable image digest, rejects critical findings according to policy, and records the exception owner when a release must proceed.
Details.errorCorrection: GuardDuty is not the ECR vulnerability scanner, security groups do not inspect image layers, and CloudFront does not modify container content.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Pre-deployment scanning shifts discovery left but needs exception, rescanning, and base-image update ownership.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: GuardDuty runtime threat detection is not the ECR image vulnerability scanner.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Network rules cannot inspect package content inside an image.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: CloudFront delivery does not remove vulnerabilities from a container image.

items.prompt: A serverless team needs vulnerability visibility for third-party packages in Lambda functions. Which service is relevant?
constraints: The function package or layer is in supported scope.
The team needs vulnerability findings rather than invocation anomaly detection.
Remediation means rebuilding or updating the dependency.

options.text: Use Amazon Inspector Lambda standard or code scanning as supported for the function and package, then update dependencies through the build process.
Use Shield because a package vulnerability is a DDoS event at the Lambda edge.
Use Route 53 because DNS health checks inspect Lambda dependency versions.
Use a security group because Lambda package contents are controlled by subnet rules.

feedback.Reason: Inspector provides supported Lambda vulnerability-scanning capabilities, while the build remains responsible for dependency remediation.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Inspector scans supported Lambda functions, layers, or code according to the selected feature and reports package or code findings. Updating the function artifact resolves the underlying issue.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team enables the needed scan, gates high-risk dependencies, and redeploys a fixed package rather than treating the finding as a network event.
Details.errorCorrection: Shield protects DDoS conditions, DNS health checks do not inspect code, and security groups do not control Lambda package content.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Managed serverless scanning improves coverage but requires package inventory, build ownership, and exception handling.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A dependency vulnerability is not a DDoS condition handled by Shield.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: DNS health checks do not inspect Lambda packages.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Security groups do not determine the code or dependency contents of a function.

items.prompt: GuardDuty raises a finding, and investigators need to understand the account, identity, IP, and resource relationships around the event. Which service adds that investigation context?
constraints: The team needs evidence exploration, not another vulnerability scan.
The finding has a known time window.
The organization can enable Detective behavior graphs.

options.text: Use Amazon Detective to explore related entities and historical behavior context, while retaining GuardDuty as a finding source.
Use Inspector because vulnerability findings automatically create a complete identity relationship graph.
Use an S3 lifecycle rule because object history is the only evidence needed for an account incident.
Use a security group because relationship graphs are built from inbound rules only.

feedback.Reason: Detective is intended for security investigation context and relationship analysis around findings.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Detective collects and models supported telemetry into behavior graphs that help analysts examine entities and activity over time. It does not replace detection or patch assessment.
Details.scenarioApplication: The investigator pivots from the GuardDuty finding into the Detective graph, compares baseline behavior, and records evidence before containment.
Details.errorCorrection: Inspector focuses on vulnerabilities, lifecycle rules do not provide account investigation context, and security groups are only one network-control input.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Behavior graphs improve investigation speed but require data sources, member-account configuration, and retention or cost review.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Inspector vulnerability findings do not provide the same relationship-focused investigation graph.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Object lifecycle history is not a complete account-entity investigation view.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Security groups alone cannot explain identity, IP, and resource behavior relationships.

items.prompt: The CISO wants one view of findings from GuardDuty, Inspector, and Config across member accounts. Which service is the central aggregation layer?
constraints: Member accounts are governed by AWS Organizations.
Source services remain enabled.
The team needs normalized findings and workflow state.

options.text: Use AWS Security Hub as the central finding aggregation and security-posture view, with source services providing their own evidence.
Use Detective as the single finding intake service because it replaces every source service.
Use CloudFormation exports because stack outputs normalize all security findings automatically.
Use one CloudWatch dashboard as the source-of-truth control plane for all finding status changes.

feedback.Reason: Security Hub aggregates and normalizes findings from supported services and partners while those services retain their detection or assessment roles.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Security Hub provides findings ingestion, standards and controls, insights, and workflow status. It is not a replacement for GuardDuty, Inspector, Detective, Config, or response automation.
Details.scenarioApplication: The delegated security administrator enables Security Hub, configures member accounts and finding integration, and assigns workflow owners.
Details.errorCorrection: Detective investigates context, CloudFormation is infrastructure state, and dashboards visualize but do not replace a finding workflow service.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Central aggregation improves triage and reporting but requires normalization, delegated administration, and noise-management policy.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Detective is an investigation service and does not replace finding aggregation from every source.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: CloudFormation outputs do not normalize runtime security findings.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A dashboard visualizes data but is not the authoritative finding workflow or integration layer.

items.prompt: A compliance team needs automated checks against a supported security standard and evidence of control status. Which Security Hub capability addresses this?
constraints: The standard is supported in the Region.
The organization will assign remediation owners.
Findings and control status must be reviewable.

options.text: Enable the applicable Security Hub security standard and controls, then manage control findings and exceptions through the defined workflow.
Use GuardDuty because threat findings are equivalent to every compliance control result.
Use WAF because web ACL rules automatically prove organization-wide control compliance.
Disable failing controls so the Security Hub score remains high and the report looks compliant.

feedback.Reason: Security Hub standards and controls evaluate supported security posture requirements and produce findings for follow-up.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Security Hub standards activate control checks and compliance findings. A score or control status is evidence for prioritization, not proof that every workload requirement is satisfied.
Details.scenarioApplication: The security administrator enables the standard, documents accepted risks, and assigns owners for failing controls rather than hiding them.
Details.errorCorrection: GuardDuty findings are not a complete compliance standard, WAF covers a web boundary, and disabling controls hides risk instead of remediating it.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Standards improve repeatable posture assessment but require scope, exception, and evidence governance.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Threat findings and compliance control results answer different questions.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: WAF protects web traffic and does not prove every organization-wide security control.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Disabling controls suppresses evidence and does not make the environment compliant.

items.prompt: A Security Hub finding is assigned to the wrong team and remains open after remediation. Which workflow design should be improved?
constraints: The source finding includes resource and account context.
Teams can update finding workflow status.
Remediation evidence must be retained.

options.text: Define finding ownership and automation by source, account, resource, severity, and control, then update workflow status only after verification evidence.
Auto-close every finding after seven days because age is proof of remediation.
Delete the source service so Security Hub stops receiving findings from that team.
Use a public spreadsheet as the workflow authority because Security Hub findings are not operational records.

feedback.Reason: Finding aggregation is useful only when ownership, status transitions, and remediation evidence are explicit.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Security Hub findings have workflow and record state that can be updated by authorized automation or users. Closing without verifying the resource leaves risk hidden.
Details.scenarioApplication: The response system routes findings to the owner, records the remediation change, and closes or reopens based on a fresh control result.
Details.errorCorrection: Finding age does not prove remediation, disabling sources removes visibility, and an uncontrolled spreadsheet is not a reliable security workflow authority.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Automation reduces triage delay but needs idempotence, exception handling, and a way to reopen recurring findings.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A finding should close after evidence of remediation, not merely after time passes.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Disabling a source hides future findings and does not remediate the resource.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A public spreadsheet can leak security data and should not replace controlled finding workflow state.

items.prompt: A security account must manage Security Hub across Organization member accounts without using the management account for daily operations. Which pattern fits?
constraints: AWS Organizations governs the accounts.
The security account is approved as delegated administrator.
Member-account findings must be aggregated with explicit scope.

options.text: Use Security Hub delegated-administrator configuration and enable or configure member accounts through the organization-wide workflow.
Use the management account root user for every finding update because delegated administration is not supported.
Use RAM to share Security Hub findings as if they were VPC subnets.
Use a public SNS topic for all findings because cross-account security data cannot remain private.

feedback.Reason: Security Hub supports organization-level administration patterns that centralize security management without normalizing root-user operations.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A delegated administrator can manage member-account Security Hub configuration and findings according to the service's organization integration. Account and Region enablement remain explicit.
Details.scenarioApplication: The security team registers the delegated administrator, enables members, and verifies findings and control status in each required Region.
Details.errorCorrection: Daily root use is unsafe, RAM is not the Security Hub administration model, and public topics are not required for private cross-account findings.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Delegated administration centralizes governance but requires organization lifecycle, Region, and permission monitoring.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Delegated administration exists to avoid routine management-account root operations.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: RAM sharing and Security Hub organization administration are different mechanisms.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Findings can be integrated through supported private service workflows without public exposure.

items.prompt: The security team wants one Region to aggregate Security Hub findings from a defined set of Regions. Which condition matters?
constraints: The selected Regions support the aggregation feature.
Security Hub is enabled in the source Regions.
The central Region is owned by the delegated administrator.

options.text: Configure cross-Region aggregation in the central Region and enable the source Regions and accounts within the documented supported scope.
Assume Security Hub findings are globally visible as soon as the service is enabled in one Region.
Use a Route 53 health check to replicate findings between Regions.
Copy finding JSON into a public S3 bucket because Region boundaries prevent private aggregation.

feedback.Reason: Security Hub cross-Region aggregation is an explicit configuration with source-Region and account prerequisites.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A home Region aggregates findings from configured linked Regions according to the service model. Regional service enablement and delegated administration remain part of the setup.
Details.scenarioApplication: The security team configures the home Region, checks source coverage, and validates that finding updates and workflow status behave as expected.
Details.errorCorrection: One-Region enablement does not create global visibility, DNS health checks do not replicate findings, and public storage is unnecessary.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Central aggregation simplifies triage but creates a regional control-plane dependency and requires careful coverage monitoring.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Security Hub resources and findings are Region-scoped until cross-Region aggregation is configured.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Route 53 health checks do not move security findings.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Supported Security Hub aggregation avoids publishing sensitive findings to public storage.

items.prompt: A recurring finding is a documented accepted risk on a non-production account. How should the team reduce noise without hiding new production findings?
constraints: The exception has an owner and expiration date.
Production resources must remain visible.
The source finding continues to exist.

options.text: Use a narrowly scoped, reviewable suppression or automation rule for the documented resource and account, with expiration and audit evidence.
Disable the entire security standard because one finding is accepted risk.
Delete the resource from the inventory so Security Hub can no longer report it.
Close every finding with the same control ID across all accounts and Regions.

feedback.Reason: Noise management should be scoped and reversible so accepted risk does not erase unrelated or future findings.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Security Hub automation and workflow controls can update or route findings according to matching criteria. Suppression or closure is not the same as remediation and needs governance.
Details.scenarioApplication: The security owner matches the non-production resource, records the reason and expiry, and reviews the exception before it lapses.
Details.errorCorrection: Disabling a standard removes broader evidence, inventory deletion hides the resource, and global control-ID closure can suppress production risk.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Scoped suppression lowers alert fatigue but creates an exception register that must be reviewed for drift and expiration.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A single accepted risk does not justify disabling an entire posture standard.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Removing inventory is a concealment action rather than a risk decision.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Control IDs can affect many resources and must not be closed globally without scope and evidence.

items.prompt: A security design must detect active credential misuse, scan container images for CVEs, investigate relationships, and aggregate findings. Which service mapping is correct?
constraints: The organization wants purpose-built managed services.
The controls remain complementary.
Findings need centralized workflow.

options.text: Use GuardDuty for threat detection, Inspector for vulnerability assessment, Detective for investigation context, and Security Hub for aggregation and posture workflow.
Use Inspector for every requirement because vulnerability scanning includes account threat detection and finding aggregation.
Use Security Hub alone because it replaces all source services and generates their underlying telemetry.
Use WAF for CVE scanning and Detective for blocking all requests before they reach an origin.

feedback.Reason: The service set is intentionally layered: detect, assess, investigate, and aggregate are different responsibilities.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: GuardDuty analyzes threat signals, Inspector assesses supported vulnerabilities, Detective provides behavior context, and Security Hub centralizes findings and controls. The organization can connect them without collapsing their roles.
Details.scenarioApplication: The security architect enables each service for its required scope and documents the finding path from detection through investigation and remediation.
Details.errorCorrection: Inspector does not cover every threat function, Security Hub does not generate every source signal by itself, and WAF or Detective do not serve the other listed roles.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Layered managed services improve coverage but add cost, integration, and ownership complexity that needs a deliberate operating model.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Inspector's vulnerability scope does not replace threat detection, investigation, or aggregation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Security Hub consumes and organizes findings; it does not replace all source telemetry services.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: WAF and Detective have different request-filtering and investigation boundaries.

items.prompt: GuardDuty reports a suspicious API call from an unfamiliar location. Which response sequence is most defensible?
constraints: The finding includes an identity and time window.
The resource is production critical.
The team must preserve evidence before containment.

options.text: Validate the finding, inspect the principal and related activity in Detective or CloudTrail, contain the credential or resource through the runbook, and record evidence.
Delete the account immediately because every GuardDuty finding proves irreversible compromise.
Ignore the finding until Inspector reports a software vulnerability on the same resource.
Change the Route 53 record because DNS updates revoke the suspicious IAM session.

feedback.Reason: A detection finding is an urgent signal requiring evidence-led validation and containment, not automatic destructive action or dismissal.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: GuardDuty identifies suspicious behavior; CloudTrail and Detective provide activity context, while IAM or workload controls perform containment. The exact action depends on the principal and resource.
Details.scenarioApplication: The responder preserves the event, disables or rotates the suspected credential when warranted, checks persistence, and tracks recovery.
Details.errorCorrection: Destructive account deletion can destroy evidence, Inspector answers a different question, and DNS changes do not revoke IAM sessions.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Fast containment reduces attacker time but should be reversible and scoped to avoid unnecessary production outage.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: A finding requires triage and scoped containment; deleting an account is destructive and disproportionate as a first step.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Threat detection and vulnerability assessment are independent signals.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: DNS changes do not revoke an IAM session or credential.

items.prompt: Auditors need to prove that high-severity security findings were triaged and remediated, while raw evidence remains protected. Which design is appropriate?
constraints: Security Hub owns the workflow view.
Source logs and investigation evidence have separate retention controls.
Only authorized responders may view sensitive evidence.

options.text: Retain finding workflow history and remediation evidence in protected destinations, map findings to owners, and restrict raw logs and graphs to least-privilege responders.
Close findings without evidence because a Security Hub score is sufficient audit proof.
Publish all finding details to a public dashboard so audit access is automatic.
Delete raw logs after closing the finding because the final status replaces the underlying event.

feedback.Reason: A finding status is useful audit metadata, but high-quality evidence also needs protected retention, ownership, and access control.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Security Hub records finding and workflow state, while CloudTrail, Detective, GuardDuty, and application logs provide underlying evidence. The stores have different sensitivity and retention requirements.
Details.scenarioApplication: The security team preserves the finding, remediation ticket, relevant logs, and verification result while limiting access to investigators and auditors.
Details.errorCorrection: A score does not prove remediation, public dashboards leak security data, and deleting raw evidence weakens investigation and auditability.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Evidence retention costs storage and access governance but supports both incident response and compliance claims.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Closing status without verification evidence is not sufficient audit proof.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Security findings and raw evidence should not be exposed through a public dashboard.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Underlying evidence may be needed for later investigation, audit, or recurrence analysis.
